origin_region: Tamil Nadu · Nilgiri Hills (Ooty, Coonoor, Kotagiri)
cultivar: Chinary and hybrid seedling bushes plus UPASI clones
processing: Fully oxidised black tea made both orthodox (whole-leaf grades) and CTC; the orthodox leaf teas are what reach speciality shops.
harvest_season: Picked all year thanks to the mild climate; the cool, dry months from December to February give the most aromatic teas.
appearance_dry: Dark brown to black, neatly twisted leaf, often with a few lighter tips.
taste_profile: Clean, fragrant and smooth: a light citrus and floral note over medium body with little astringency, which is why it stays clear when iced.

brewing.notes: Just under the boil, 3–4 minutes, milk optional. The classic iced-tea leaf: it does not cloud when chilled.

vintage_note: Sold year-round through the Coonoor and Coimbatore auctions, mostly as CTC and broken grades, with orthodox leaf grades (OP, FOP, TGFOP) from estates such as Glendale, Havukal, Chamraj, Kodanad and Craigmore going to export. Winter lots (December–February) are the ones to look for; buy the current season and use within a year or two. Nilgiri orthodox carries a geographical indication and the Tea Board's Nilgiri logo.
description:
Nilgiri tea comes from the Nilgiri Hills, the 'Blue Mountains' of Tamil Nadu in southern India, where tea grows between roughly 1,000 and 2,500 metres on steep slopes around Ooty, Coonoor and Kotagiri. It is India's third great black tea after Assam and Darjeeling and the least known of the three, partly because so much of it has disappeared into blends and tea bags.

The hills have a mild climate without a real winter, so the bushes are plucked all year. Most of the crop is CTC for the Indian market and for export, but the orthodox leaf teas made by estates such as Glendale, Havukal, Chamraj, Kodanad and Craigmore are what interest speciality drinkers. They are fully oxidised, neatly twisted and bright.

The cup is clean, fragrant and smooth: a light citrus and floral note over medium body, with far less astringency than Assam and none of Darjeeling's sharpness. That low tannin is why Nilgiri is the classic iced-tea leaf: it stays clear when it cools instead of turning cloudy. Brew it with water just under the boil for three to four minutes, with or without milk.

It is sold year-round through the Coonoor and Coimbatore auctions, mostly in broken and CTC grades, with orthodox leaf grades (OP, FOP, TGFOP) from named estates going to export. The cool, dry months from December to February give the most aromatic teas, sold as winter or 'frost' lots; buy the current season and use it within a year or two. Nilgiri orthodox has a geographical indication and the Tea Board's Nilgiri logo.

It is also one of the best-value black teas around: a single-estate Nilgiri often costs less than a comparable Ceylon.
